theme: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 1. It is the doorway to the whole Psalter. Read it slowly, and notice the contrast between two ways of life.
settingTheScene: Psalm 1 has no title and no named author, and it serves as the introduction to the Psalter. It places two ways in front of every reader: the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. It begins with the word “blessed,” the same word that opens many of the most important sections of Scripture. After the story of Eli’s sons and Israel’s failure, the psalm shows what a blessed life looks like.
observation: “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers” (v. 1).
“But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night” (v. 2).
“He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither” (v. 3).
“In all that he does, he prospers” (v. 3).
“The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away” (v. 4).
“Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous” (v. 5).
“For the LORD knows the way of the righteous” (v. 6).
“But the way of the wicked will perish” (v. 6).
interpretation:
Psalm 1 uses three verbs in verse 1 for the downward slide of the wicked: walk, stand, sit. A person first walks with the wicked, then stands in their way, then settles in as one of them. The slide is gradual. The first step is to take their counsel. It starts with what we listen to.

The positive picture is a tree. The righteous person is rooted in God’s word. His delight is in the law of the LORD, and he meditates on it day and night. The word “meditates” means to mutter or murmur, to go over the words quietly again and again. It is the opposite of casual reading. The tree is planted by streams of water, and its roots go deep, so that it bears fruit in season and does not wither.

Verse 3 says, “In all that he does, he prospers.” This must be read carefully. It does not promise worldly success in every case. The psalms themselves show righteous people suffering. It describes the fruit of a rooted life, and it points to the ultimate outcome. A person planted by the water will be fruitful, even if the fruit is not always visible.

The wicked are like chaff, the dry, weightless husk that the wind blows away. They have no root and no substance. The contrast is between weight and lightness, depth and surface. Verse 6 gives the reason behind it all: “The LORD knows the way of the righteous.” This is covenant knowledge. He watches over them and cares for them. The way of the wicked perishes because it leads nowhere.

Psalm 1 sets the tone for everything that follows. The Psalter is the prayer book of those who delight in God’s word. The key is the law of the LORD, which at this point in the story is the book of Moses, and which will be fulfilled in the one who perfectly kept it.
connection: Jesus is the truly blessed man who never walked in the counsel of the wicked and who delighted in the Father’s will (John 4:34). Jeremiah 17:7-8 echoes the tree image, and Revelation 22:2 shows the tree of life by the river. Jesus said, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5). Paul says that we are “rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17), and “rooted and built up in him” (Colossians 2:7).
application:
Ask whose counsel you listen to most. Is there a voice you need to turn down?

Choose a short passage to meditate on throughout the day. Return to it often.

Thank God that he knows your way.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to be a tree planted by his streams.
Ask him to root you in his word and keep you from the counsel of the wicked.
Thank him that he knows your way.
